cultivar: Local old-tree types including Benshan, Ergazi and Heitiaozi
processing: Made as raw pu-erh usually is: wilted, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose. Lots mix several old-tree types unless stated otherwise.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual prized picking, as across Lincang.
appearance_dry: Long dark green strips, varying with the mix of old-tree types in the lot.
appearance_wet: Yellow-green leaves whose shape varies with the tree type.
taste_profile: Little is recorded in plain tasting terms. As with other Lincang raw teas, expect a sweet, full cup with some bitterness, and differences between single-type lots.

brewing.notes: Try single-type lots side by side when you can; that is the reason to seek this mountain out.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as loose mao cha or pressed cakes, usually young spring tea. It is cheap for an old-tree origin: one spring list had mixed-picked material at 200 to 350 yuan a kilo. Ask whether a lot is mixed or from one tree type, since 'old tree' here covers a wide range.
description:
Baiyingshan sits in the middle of the Dabingshan range at Manwan town in Yun County, facing the Wuliang Mountains across the Lancang River. Its gardens are the draw: wild, semi-wild and cultivated old trees grow together around dozens of hamlets, and it is often called a living museum of tea plants.

The leaf is not one thing. Local types named Benshan, Ergazi and Heitiaozi all grow here, and most material is made in the normal raw pu-erh way, which means the mix affects the cup a great deal.

Plain tasting notes for the mountain are few. As with other Lincang raw teas, expect sweetness and fullness with some bitterness. Brew it hot with short steeps and vary the time between lots.

The price is the surprise: mixed-picked tea costs little next to Mengku's famous villages. Large numbers in promotional material, such as tree counts and ages, deserve some caution, so judge by the cup.
history:
Local accounts describe gardens between 1,800 and 2,300 metres with about 1.8 million wild, semi-wild and cultivated old trees, and claim the oldest is over 2,400 years old. These figures come from regional promotion and have not been independently tested.

The mountain's modern reputation has grown along with the pu-erh market; a garden museum and a tea workshop have been set up on site. Its scientific interest lies in the range of tree types growing side by side.
